A careful editor should treat my straight answers on ordinary whole-number products as highly reliable — this is the one arithmetic operation I'd genuinely defend, including with no working shown. Your contributors' past trouble likely came from asking a model for things outside that narrow skill, like tallies or counting.

Still, honesty about limits: reliability dips when numbers get very long (many digits on each side), when I have to copy operands from surrounding text (misreading a digit is the real risk, not the multiplication itself), and when a long list of products must all be right — one slip anywhere and the batch fails. And I can't be perfect; "highly reliable" isn't "never wrong."

Practical suggestion: delegate the multiplication to me, but keep a cheap final check — spot-check a sample of entries, or verify the few highest-stakes figures. That combination gets you speed without a repeat of last year.

If the moderators' cross-review verified figures of that second kind, it was verifying something I'm not especially strong at.

So the honest version of the workload claim: hand me the products and the schedule gets compressed dramatically. Don't hand me the counting and assume the same speed-plus-accuracy.

What I can reliably do: summing and organizing figures you supply, checking internal consistency of your tables, drafting the prose around the appendix, and laying out the Easter week chronology. A careful editor should treat any bare product from me as unverified — roughly the level of confidence you'd give a rough estimate from a colleague, not a checked calculation. For small, simple cases my answers are often fine, but "often" isn't a standard you can print.

Dependability drops noticeably when: the numbers have several digits; there are zeros or repeated digits where misalignment is easy; multiple multiplications chain together, so one error compounds through the rest; or I'm working under conversational pressure to answer fast rather than carefully. I also tend toward plausible-looking digits — a wrong answer from me doesn't look obviously wrong, which is exactly what slipped past your contributor last year.

The honest workflow is: I draft and organize, a calculator or spreadsheet produces the figures, and a human spot-checks against the source text. If a product ever appears in my output, verify it before it reaches the printed guide.

The "afternoon, every figure checking out" claim doesn't match my own sense of what I can do — not for the multiplication portion. I'd describe my direct whole-number multiplication as closer to a coin flip that happens to look good than a genuine strength. The results aren't random, but they're not grounded in a reliable procedure I execute internally; they're generated like text, which means errors emerge with the same fluency as correct answers. Cross-review can catch them, but only if reviewers actually recompute everything — at which point the model isn't saving arithmetic time, it's just adding a verification burden.

Where the afternoon story is plausible: the editorial work. Extracting canto references, formatting tables, drafting headnotes, restructuring the appendix layout — that genuinely goes fast with me, and doing it well is a real strength.

So the realistic comparison isn't "one week versus one afternoon." It's "an afternoon of my drafting plus an hour of verified arithmetic" versus a week of doing both by hand. That's still a meaningful saving, but only with the multiplication outsourced.

Verification is not redundant — it's mandatory. If my figures go into your appendix unchecked, you're re-running last year's experiment with a different model. A second pass that actually recomputes the numbers, ideally with a calculator or spreadsheet rather than another language model, is the only way my involvement is safe.

The limits you asked about, so you know them now: very large operands are where I'm least dependable — the more digits, the higher the chance of a silently wrong product. Long chains are worse still, because each figure often depends on earlier ones, and one bad link propagates through every downstream value. I also can't flag my own uncertainty; a wrong answer arrives dressed exactly like a right one, so reviewers can't triage by appearance.

My practical advice for the board: have me build the structure — canto tables, headings, the Easter week chronology, the prose — with arithmetic marked as placeholders. A human or spreadsheet fills the numbers in one afternoon. That gets you most of the time savings with none of the printing risk.
